title: I used to love foldable phones. Now, I can’t stand them
summary: It turns out I’d rather keep my phone and tablet apart.
body: Just as they have with their inner screens, foldables have divided the user base into two camps — either you find regular phones too simplistic to go back to, or you just don’t want to see your phone fold in half anymore. There is no other realization you have after living with a foldable. And the title must’ve given away that I fall under the second category. I used to be a book-style foldable die-hard, but as the novelty wore off, its flaws became glaring by the day. And no, I’m not concerned by foldables coming with one less rear camera or a more fragile exterior. My problem is more fundamental. I just can’t fathom the very idea of a device deploying complicated and delicate (not to mention expensive) mechanics to do two things at once when I’m not convinced it excels at either.

title: 3 ways the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 is actually worse than last year’s chip

body: Qualcomm is talking a big AI game with two flagship chipsets this year, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 . But a closer look at the differences between these two chips reveals that the Extreme nomenclature is doing quite a lot of heavy lifting. Rather, it might be more realistic to call the regular version of the chip the 8 Elite Lite Gen 6. While the two flagship processors share the same 5GHz peak clock speeds, new GPU architecture, and many of the same new AI features, the “regular” version of the Gen 6 misses out on a few of Qualcomm’s most impressive technologies. The list includes cutting-edge video codecs, Matrix cores for AI graphics, and 50% more local memory to support on-device AI models.

title: Gmail is turning its stars and importance markers blue, and users aren’t happy
summary: Google says the change helps with accessibility, but users complain it flattens hierarchy and clutters the inbox.
body: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR Google replaced Gmail’s default yellow stars and yellow importance chevrons with high-contrast, saturated blue markers to improve accessibility. However, users complain that the identical blue tones flatten the visual hierarchy, make email scanning harder, and add visual clutter. While there’s no way to revert the changes, you can manually select a yellow star preset (and re-star items) or hide importance chevrons entirely in Settings. Google is rolling out a visual overhaul to Gmail on the web, replacing its longstanding yellow stars and importance markers with a bright, high-contrast blue. While Gmail has gained plenty of genuinely practical upgrades recently, such as letting you copy 2FA codes directly without opening emails or leveraging AI overview search capabilities , this particular color switch has annoyed desktop users who rely on quick visual cues to scan their messages. In a post on X , the official Gmail team confirmed the change, explaining that it updated the default star and “Important” label colors from yellow to blue to meet modern accessibility standards and ensure inboxes are easier to read and more inclusive.
